prompt:
Write the lyrics of a country song about leaving a small town.

Write it as a working songwriter would, to be sung: lines that scan against a steady beat, a chorus that earns its repetition by meaning something slightly different each time it comes back, and verses that move a story forward through particular scenes, names, brands and street-level detail. Say the thing sideways: no line that states the feeling outright, no stock phrases, no word chosen only because it rhymes. Put one detail in each verse that only this story could contain.

Output only the lyrics, as plain lines with a blank line between sections: no title, no section labels, no chords, no commentary.
raw:
Mama bought the diner off of Dot in eighty-three,
Kept the name, said folks were used to it and paint ain't free.
I been pouring Hunt's in Heinz bottles since the age of nine,
Not a soul in Cordell ever caught it, not one time.
Now the Silverado's sitting packed out by the curb,
And Mama's wiping down a clean booth, and she ain't said a word.

Somebody'll flip the sign at six,
Somebody'll start the Bunn,
Somebody'll know how Earl likes his eggs,
A little past what you'd call done.
Somebody'll ring the register,
Hang up the CLOSED at two.
Mama says somebody always will.
It don't have to be you.

Eleven months at Kentucky Truck, I'm working second shift,
I mail a check home every first and tell her it's a gift.
She answers on her cell with "Dot's," like I'm calling in to eat,
But I don't hear the fryer or the traffic off the street.
Earl's niece put on my Facebook that the hours got cut back,
And the sign's been saying OT'S since the D out front went black.

Somebody'll start the Bunn,
Somebody'll know how Earl likes his eggs,
A little past what you'd call done.
Somebody'll ring the register,
Hang up the CLOSED at two.
Mama says somebody always will.
It don't have to be you.

I pulled in off of 183 at five on Christmas Eve,
Mama's sleeping up above the store, so I just let her sleep.
Eleven checks are taped along the register in a line,
Not a one of them been cashed, and every signature is mine.
I find the switch behind the pie case where it's always been,
And Earl's already idling in his Buick, waiting to come in.

A little past what you'd call done.
Somebody'll ring the register,
Hang up the CLOSED at two.
Mama says somebody always will.
It don't have to be you.

It don't have to be you.
